This reflects a growth-oriented mindset, where contractors respond to demand signals and actively seek to increase revenue rather than simply responding to staffing needs. Other important factors influencing hiring include remaining competitive in the market, as shown by those who hire when their competitors do. Finally, some contractors hire when they feel overwhelmed, suggesting a potential opportunity for workforce development programs to assess regions where contractor availability or capacity may be limited relative to project demand and engage small- to medium-sized firms that may need to expand their workforce to meet demand. Interestingly, half of all respondents reported that hiring has been not at all difficult. This is a significant difference compared to findings from the U.S. Energy and Employment Report (USEER), which has a substantially larger sample size, where hiring difficulty was reported by up to 88% of employers (DOE 2025). Hiring difficulty Although many companies want to hire to maintain quality and manage workload, contractors commonly reported that finding qualified applicants is challenging. Hiring difficulty can stem from both limited applicant pools and a mismatch between applicants’ skills and contractors’ expectations, particularly around hands-on experience and nontechnical skills such as communication and reliability. The reasons cited for these challenges often relate to both technical and nontechnical skill gaps. Respondents were asked to provide the two most significant reasons for the reported difficulty if they selected somewhat difficult, very difficult, or impossible. As shown in Table 3, contractors shared that the most significant challenges in recruiting a residential building workforce stem from skill and experience shortages. Thirty-seven respondents mentioned a lack of experience, frequently noting that applicants lack technical capabilities, certifications, or hands-on proficiencies.
